name: Link My Books
description: It turns Amazon, eBay, Shopify, Etsy, and other shop payouts into a short, VAT-correct entry in Xero or QuickBooks, matched to the money that actually hit the bank. Founded 2018 in the UK. A2X, in New Zealand since 2014, does the same job for Shopify, Amazon, BigCommerce, Etsy, Walmart, and eBay, into QuickBooks, Xero, and Sage. Jamie McDonald is A2X's CEO.

mentions.evidence: GetLatka's September 2025 estimate for Link My Books is about $660,000 a year, with 6 employees. The site, checked 5 November 2026, says it is trusted by 10,000+ businesses in the UK, the US, and Australia, and by hundreds of accounting firms. Plans run from $24 a month for 1 channel and 200 orders, and $47 for 1,000 orders, up to $380 for 10 channels and 30,000 orders. A2X has a separate GetLatka estimate from July 2025 of about $7.3 million a year, with 66 employees.
mentions.indieAngle: A2X is the bigger product and Link My Books is the smaller one, in the same job. The gap the note points at is narrower still: one marketplace, one ledger, one country.

whyItPrints: A marketplace payout is a pile of fees, refunds, reserves, and currencies. The accountant does not want to type that by hand. Once a client's books are wired up, they tend to stay. The price follows how many orders the seller has, so the bill grows when the seller grows.
whyThisMatters: A marketplace does not pay a seller a clean invoice. It pays a lump that already had fees, refunds, reserves, and a currency change taken out. The accountant's job is to make that lump match the bank. Doing it by hand is how a small firm loses a day. Link My Books writes one summary into Xero or QuickBooks and ties it to the deposit. The price steps up with channels and with order count, so a busier seller pays more without anyone renegotiating a seat. It started in the UK in 2018. The site says thousands of businesses and hundreds of firms use it. A2X has been doing the same job since 2014, from New Zealand, for a longer list of shops and for Sage as well as the two ledgers. The two yearly figures in the note are both estimates, taken months apart, and they are not the same business. One is a six-person company. The other is much larger. That is the whole comparison.
